{{Short description|Rule of replacement in propositional logic}}
{{Infobox mathematical statement
| name = Exportation
| type = [[Rule of replacement]]
| field = [[Propositional calculus]]
| statement = 
| symbolic statement = <math>((P \land Q) \to R) \Leftrightarrow (P \to (Q \to R))</math>
}}
{{Transformation rules}}

'''Exportation'''<ref>{{cite book |title=A Concise Introduction to Logic 4th edition |last=Hurley |first=Patrick |year=1991 |publisher=Wadsworth Publishing |pages=364–5 |isbn=9780534145156 |url=https://archive.org/details/studyguidetoacco00burc|url-access=registration }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Copi |first1=Irving M. |last2=Cohen |first2=Carl |title=Introduction to Logic |publisher=Prentice Hall |year=2005 |page=371 }}</ref><ref>Moore and Parker</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.philosophypages.com/lg/e11b.htm|title=Rules of Replacement}}</ref> is a [[Validity (logic)|valid]] [[rule of replacement]] in [[propositional logic]]. The rule allows [[material conditional|conditional statement]]s having [[Logical conjunction|conjunctive]] [[antecedent (logic)|antecedent]]s to be replaced by statements having conditional [[consequent]]s and vice versa in [[formal proof|logical proofs]]. It is the rule that:

:<math>((P \land Q) \to R) \Leftrightarrow (P \to (Q \to R))</math>

Where "<math>\Leftrightarrow</math>" is a [[metalogic]]al [[Symbol (formal)|symbol]] representing "can be replaced in a proof with." In strict terminology, <math>((P \land Q) \to R) \Rightarrow (P \to (Q \to R))</math> is the law of exportation, for it "exports" a proposition from the antecedent of <math>(P \land Q) \to R</math> to its consequent. Its converse, the law of '''importation''', <math>(P \to (Q \to R))\Rightarrow ((P \land Q) \to R) </math>, "imports" a proposition from the consequent of <math>P \to (Q \to R)</math> to its antecedent.

== Formal notation ==
The ''exportation'' rule may be written in [[sequent]] notation:
:<math>((P \land Q) \to R) \dashv\vdash (P \to (Q \to R))</math>

where <math>\dashv\vdash</math> is a metalogical symbol meaning that <math>(P \to (Q \to R))</math> is a [[Logical equivalence|syntactic equivalent]] of <math>((P \land Q) \to R)</math> in some [[formal system|logical system]];

or in [[inference rule|rule form]]:
:<math>\frac{(P \land Q) \to R}{P \to (Q \to R)}</math>, <math>\frac{P \to (Q \to R)}{(P \land Q) \to R}.</math>

where the rule is that wherever an instance of "<math>(P \land Q) \to R</math>" appears on a line of a proof, it can be replaced with "<math>P \to (Q \to R)</math>", and vice versa.

[[Import-export (logic)|Import-export]] is a name given to the statement as a [[theorem]] or truth-functional [[Tautology (logic)|tautology]] of propositional logic:

:<math>((P \land Q) \to R) \leftrightarrow (P \to (Q \to R))</math>

where <math>P</math>, <math>Q</math>, and <math>R</math> are propositions expressed in some [[logical system]].

== Natural language ==

=== Example ===
It rains and the sun shines implies that there is a rainbow. <br>
Thus, if it rains, then the sun shines implies that there is a rainbow.

If my car is on, when I switch the gear to D the car starts going.
If my car is on and I have switched the gear to D, then the car must start going.

== Proof == 

The following proof uses a [[classical logic|classically]] valid chain of equivalences. Rules used are [[material implication (rule of inference)|material implication]], [[De Morgan's law]], and the [[associative property]] of [[disjunction (logic)|disjunction]].

{| class="wikitable"
! ''Proposition''
! ''Derivation''
|-
| <math> P\rightarrow (Q\rightarrow R)</math> || Given 
|-
| <math>\neg P \lor  (Q \rightarrow R)</math> ||[[material implication (rule of inference)|material implication]]
|-
| <math>\neg P \lor (\neg Q \lor R)</math> || material implication
|-
|<math>(\neg P \lor \neg Q) \lor R</math>  || [[associativity]]
|-
|<math> \neg (P \land Q) \lor R</math>|| [[De Morgan's law]]
|-
| <math>(P \land Q) \rightarrow R</math> || material implication 
|}

Due to the use of [[material implication (rule of inference)|material implication]] in the first two steps, this is not an intuitionistically valid proof.

==Relation to functions==
Exportation is associated with [[currying]] via the [[Curry–Howard correspondence]].{{cn|date=November 2023}}
